query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an ultra‐thin, coherent interfacial layer via nanometer‐scale surface modification on high‐entropy alloy intermediate layers will improve heat-transfer capability while preserving their structural integrity under plasma‐facing reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloy intermediate layers currently optimized for mechanical robustness but exhibiting suboptimal thermal conductivity.
generation.intervention: Deposit or induce an engineered coherent interfacial layer (e.g., via controlled nanometer-scale surface modification) on the alloy to improve the connectivity of thermal transport paths.
generation.conditions: Under reactor-simulated conditions including high temperatures (approximately 600–1000°C) and cyclic mechanical and thermal loading typical of plasma-facing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The ultra-thin coherent interfacial layer at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The interfacial layer reduces phonon and electron scattering at grain boundaries, thereby creating continuous, low-resistance thermal conduction paths while not altering the bulk composition that ensures mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified high-entropy alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in thermal conductivity (improved heat-transfer capability) comparable to, or better than, current intermediate-layer performance while maintaining its high strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Performance data from existing high-entropy alloy intermediate layers used in plasma-facing components that prioritize mechanical integrity but have limited heat-transfer performance.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated within the operational temperature range (600–1000°C) and under standard cyclic mechanical and thermal loads; performance under extreme conditions (e.g., very high irradiation doses or uncharacteristic thermal cycling beyond tested ranges) remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal conductivity improvement is uncertain, and long-term stability of the engineered interfacial layer under actual reactor irradiation and flux conditions requires further experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy intermediate-layer samples: one set with the engineered ultra-thin coherent interfacial layer and one control set without the modification. Subject both sets to reactor-simulated conditions (600–1000°C with cyclic thermal and mechanical loading). Afterwards, perform comparative analyses of thermal conductivity (using techniques such as laser flash analysis) and mechanical integrity (via tensile testing and hardness measurements).
measurements: Thermal conductivity before and after exposure
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM) to assess the integrity and coherence of the interfacial layer
Mechanical properties including tensile strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the engineered interfacial layer do not show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity compared to the control, or if their mechanical properties degrade relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the present study, the thermophysical properties (thermal conductivity and volumetric specific heat capacity) of the CoCrFeNiCu HEA are systematically investigated via the MD method. A series of MD simulations are performed to explore the influencing factors (e.g., temperature and chemical composition) that may affect the thermal conductivity and the volumetric specific heat capacity of the CoCrFeNiCu HEA. Furthermore, phonon density of states (PDOS) analysis is conducted to understand how the influencing factors affect the heat transfer of HEAs. This research provides theoretical foundations for the design and optimisation of new HEA materials.

It also confirms the presence of well mixed surface sites on the HEA catalysts and suggests that the experimentally observed scaling relationship between the nanoparticle composition and the surface adsorption property can be understood via the surface site mixing mechanism,. It should be noted that our atomistic modeling results are consistent with the prediction based on simple thermodynamic calculations, confirming the tendency of the given quinary composition to form a single solid-solution phase. More importantly, the structural similarity at the different temperatures (from 573 to 1000 K) underlines the high thermal stability of the HEA nanoparticles, consistent with the observation from the catalytic durability studies (see Table 2).

decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys for extreme conditions focused on achieving high strength, ductility, and thermal stability primarily through compositional tuning and microstructural refinement (e.g., fabrication of nanocrystalline films and pillar compression studies). Later studies, such as the stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations approach, further advanced the ability to tailor the internal architecture to mediate dislocation transmission and enhance both strength and ductility at high temperatures. In all these cases, the innovations have centered on preserving or even enhancing structural integrity under high‐temperature and high‐stress conditions but have not directly targeted an improvement in heat-transfer capability.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge remains to break the longstanding trade-off between mechanical robustness and thermal conductivity in intermediate high‐entropy alloy layers for plasma-facing reactor components. Specifically, while prior interventions have succeeded in consolidating mechanical performance, they have not addressed the potential for optimizing interfacial or microstructural features to actively enhance heat-transfer without compromising structural integrity.
decision.lever: Engineered coherent interfacial layers (e.g., via nanometer-scale surface modification) designed to reduce phonon/electron scattering at grain boundaries
decision.why: Given the trend of successfully using microstructural control (such as nanoprecipitations) to maintain high strength and ductility, the next logical step is to exploit surface/interface engineering. By depositing or inducing ultra-thin, well-bonded interfacial layers that are highly conductive, the thermal paths within the alloy can be enhanced without altering the bulk composition. Such an intervention directly addresses the key limitation (suboptimal heat-transfer) under plasma-facing conditions, while leveraging established strengths in microstructural design.
